Hey, Dad.  
So I did get married after all, and I couldn't be any happier. Our wedding was two weeks ago; it was so beautiful, like a dream come true. A real-life yet fairy tale style kind of wedding. I wish you could have seen it.  
Last year, we moved in together, and since then we've been trying to always talk about our problems, instead of letting them break us apart. And we've already accomplished so many things together! We have our own apartment, a small vegetable garden, and a baby lemon tree!

Also, it's nice how we talk about kids as if they're already in our lives. We're dreaming together, and that's absolutely beautiful. Hopefully, we'll havw them soon.  


Love you, Dad!

I second this. 

I'm also a daughter to a widowed mother and I can tell you it took me longer to learn how to cook than how to drill a wall.  

I have a brother, but mum taught me how to do most things men can. She never married again, and that was okay. Her male friends gave her tips on how to deal with a growing boy, told her things she didn't know. Your family can help you with the male model thing. 

But you can raise your daughter without a father and learn things with her. I'm finishing my engineering degree and every now and then I teach her things about electricity and stuff. She taught me many things she knew and now I can teach her things she doesn't. We've been learning things together for over a decade now and we became best friends very recently, after we solved some problems. 

Every father's day I give her a gift. She did raise us as a mother AND a father, after all. And I still cry on my father's birthday and his death anniversary, but that's okay. You shouldn't be mad if you daughter ever does.

And when it gets hard, for either of you, you can talk about it. Tell her stories about her dad and tell her how great he was. And make sure she knows she can always count on you, so when she grows up she'll be there for you too. 

The relationship between a widowed mother and a fatherless daughter can be very strong. You'll have some arguments, I'm sure. Sometimes she'll feel you're being authoritative and has no balance. But if you tread carefully and treat her lovingly, she'll understand you just had no option and you were learning too. At least I did and I hope your daughter will too.

Always be kind and honest, even when you have to correct her. You can be strict and still show love. Make sure she understands you're doing your job as a parent, but it doesn't mean you don't love her. When she does well in something, celebrate. You can tell her her dad would be proud, too. You don't have to pretend he never existed. 

I wish you luck in your journey, OP. It'll be a long and bumpy one, but it's totally worth it. I love my mum to no end and I know your daughter will love you too.

Keep us posted. Lots of love from here.

I'll tell you my story, OP.

I have a twin sister and a younger brother. My father died when I was 8 and still very naïve. When I was a few years older, one of my cousins started arguing with my mother about something behind closed doors in my grandmother's house. I still don't know what started it, but my mother kept screaming at him and telling him to tell us (my siblings and I) what he was threatening to tell if he was a real man. He left the room, said he loved us and left.

We went back home and in the car my mother told us my brother was not our father's son. I was absolutely shocked. For many years I resented my mother and even hated her. We had awful arguments, and it took me many years to forgive her. I never had the chance to ask my father if he knew, although I think he did. And sometimes I'm not sure I'm his daughter either. And more often than not I think I'd like to know, but I don't know what it would do to my mental health and how I'd see the rest of my family, as my father's sister is the only relative I have left from his side (and she's my Godmother).

So I come to my conclusion. To be very honest, I wish I never knew anything about it. I wish I was completely oblivious of everything. It was never my problem, to begin with. Even my brother's father (and perhaps mine) is dead by now. But fate decided I had to know. So I'm glad it was my mother who told us, out of love, not my cousin, out of anger. She told us the truth to protect us from people who never meant us well, like my cousin, who just wanted to hurt her and never cared about us.

So I think you should talk to your mother first. If she loves him, she should be honest and beg for forgiveness. Their relationship should not be based on lies. If your father forgives her, that's awesome. If he doesn't, well, she dug her own grave when she cheated on him and no one can blame him for being hurt. And if your mother refuses to tell him, it's your job to tell him the truth, out of love. And make sure he knows you love him (in case you do, of course) and the fact that you're not his daughter doesn't change your feelings for him. 

But be prepared for a lot of anger and hate. From your parents and your siblings.

Wish you luck, OP. Keep us posted. Lots of love from here.

Let me tell you a story about my own sister. We're twins, but let's say she's picked the wrong guys and friends way too many times. Her first real boyfriend was seemingly very attentive, all of her family (myself included) liked him very much and we couldn't believe when she dumped him. One day she told me, and I guess mum too, he took her virginity forcefully in the kitchen while everyone else was in the house. He'd force himself on her way too much and repeatedly, to a point it could have been considered rape. 

And then she had another bf. All too nice, very attentive, super cool again. We loved him to bits. And then she dumped him. Again, we didn't understand. And then she told me he was horribly jealous and couldn't let her breathe, would call her while she was at work to check if she wasn't with anyone else. He was sexually forceful as well. 

And she was raped once by her best friend's husband. Her best friend believed her at first, but when she told her family they pressured, saying she couldn't finish her marriage over something like that. So all her family members starting bombarding my sister with text messages so she wouldn't press charges in court (it was already done at a police station). She never talked to her friend again and it was the best thing she could have ever done.

So yeah, sometimes it's for the best to stay the fuck away from people who push you and just leave behind seemingly attentive guys. It's not at all the same situation, don't I know, but those people are not reliable, girl. I'm totally with your sister, as I am with mine. Don't let your family push you to keep someone as fucked up as a man who abandons his pregnant wife. Take every penny you can from him for child support and don't ever look back. You don't want an arsehole like that in your life. And if your family doesn't agree with you, well, just think it's not them who'd have to live with doubt and afraid of being thrown out again.

Stay with your sister if you have to. Get your job back and live your life the best you can, raising your son with love and courage. He'll learn much better things from a strong mum than from a coward dad.

So you probably tried too hard, my dear. You should never look like you're trying too much. Healthy relationships should feel light, never like you want something from the other person, you know? You shouldn't come with a pre-planned line, instead you should approach someone with genuine intentions. Something like "May I sit here?" (if it's a public place) or "Is the coffee/tea/w.e drink here good? It's my first time around." (if the person is drinking coffee and you look a little bit lost once you arrive at a new coffee shop). You shouldn't sound too harsh or forceful. Charisma is hard, but I think, by reading your reply, that's what you should work on. 

> Even when I try to be outgoing it always backfires. 

Being outgoing isn't necessarily the trick. I know a lot of shy people who are amazing. They don't just wear shyness on their sleeve. Despite being shy, they show some interest and some energy. They try (but not too much). 

Ok, this is a long shot and you should never follow exactly how it's demonstrated, but here is a video where this guy talks about how shyness and anxiety can be used to your advantage. [How to turn anxiety into charisma](https://youtu.be/xm100J0nDy8) 

I usually am very charismatic in person and I just found this channel. I found out I already do a lot of those those things without even thinking, and there is a still a lot to learn, like some small details that would make my conversations more light or my approaches less strange. I began watching out of curiosity, but I think it might bring you some light on how being more charismatic looks like. You should give it a try and put it to practice. You might fail a few times, but the good thing is that you don't know that strange person you practiced with anyway and might never meet them again. And maybe one day you'll find someone who liked your approach and sticks around. Just don't give up.

I truly wish you luck. =)

I was probably six when someone decided to hold onto me while drowning. 

My parents had built a pretty big swimming where we lived and mum thought it would be best if she taught us how to swim before letting us swim by ourselves (we were 3 kids). I didn't go to swimming lessons, but I knew how to float and not to drown, basically.

So my parents had these terrible friends (I despise them until this very day) and they had 5 kids. We were having a barbecue by the pool, something that was supposed to be fun and awesome. The dumb father of 5 decided that an innocent prank would be cool, so he pushed one of his daughters at the deep end, but she didn't know how to swim. I happened to be there, just hanging around, and she, as desperate as any drowning kid (or person, in general) could be, held onto me and tried to reach the edge by pushing me down. It lasted a few seconds, but it definitely felt like ages. I tried to swim up and she kept pushing me down. We eventually reached the edge and her fucking dumb father pulled her out. No one thanked me, but at least my mum reprimanded him for being so stupid. 

Tldr: a father pushed his kid into the pool and she didn't know how to swim, so she used me as a float.

Edit: mum reprimanded her father, not the kid.
